title: A no to the EU, not to Europe: What Icelanders actually voted on – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Iceland's 52.8%-47.2% vote against resuming EU accession talks is being misread by Europe's far-right as an anti-EU landslide, when the real drivers were fisheries sovereignty, currency skepticism and a US-growth-envy narrative - not a rejection of Iceland's already-deep European integration via the EEA.

insights.claim: Iceland voted 52.8% to 47.2% against resuming EU accession negotiations, but this does not represent a vote against Europe since Iceland already sits inside the single market via the EEA, is in Schengen, and adopts most EU legislation to stay compliant with Brussels standards.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: European far-right politicians (Farage, Le Pen) are citing this vote as evidence of anti-EU momentum, but investors reading it as a genuine sovereignty/populist realignment signal would be mispricing the actual driver.
insights.quote: Iceland did not vote against Europe—it voted to keep the Europe it already has.

insights.claim: Official Icelandic government survey data shows only 6% of Icelanders believe international cooperation diminishes national sovereignty versus 69% who believe it strengthens it, and 58% view the EEA agreement positively versus 19% negatively.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Contradicts the international narrative of a sovereigntist backlash; Icelandic public opinion remains strongly pro-integration in substance even while rejecting formal membership.

insights.claim: Iceland's political culture (Pride parade as its biggest annual festival, women holding the presidency, premiership, foreign ministry, national church bishopric, capital mayoralty, police chief and both major university deanships) makes it a poor fit for the anti-liberal-democracy movements the far-right is trying to associate it with.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Undercuts the far-right framing of Iceland's vote as ideologically aligned with European nationalist movements.
insights.locator: The Icelandic electorate has never shown much enthusiasm

themes.theme: Fisheries as the real veto point

insights.claim: Accepting the EU's common fisheries policy is a de facto requirement for full membership and is a non-negotiable red line for most Icelanders, rooted in the 1975 'cod wars' victory that expanded Iceland's fishing zone against British opposition and is a core source of national pride.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Fisheries sovereignty is the structural ceiling on any future Icelandic EU membership push, regardless of economic or security conditions - a durable constraint for any renewed accession bid.
insights.quote: For most Icelanders, this is where the conversation stops.

insights.claim: Iceland's 2009 EU accession application stalled and was shelved specifically because Brussels never gave a clear answer on whether Iceland could secure a fisheries carve-out, and this unresolved question - not ideology - made a no vote logical even for people who don't object to membership in principle.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Any future EU-Iceland accession talks will likely stall again on the same unresolved fisheries question unless the EU pre-commits to a carve-out.
insights.quote: Why board a train if you do not believe it will reach its destination?
insights.locator: The application launched in 2009 produced no answer

insights.claim: Iceland's króna has lost 99.9% of its value against the Danish krone since being pegged at parity in 1918, and major internationally active Icelandic businesses have already largely abandoned it in favor of the euro as their operating currency, despite Iceland remaining outside the eurozone.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Currency weakness is already being arbitraged away by large Icelandic corporates independent of EU membership status, suggesting de facto euroization at the corporate level regardless of the referendum outcome.
insights.locator: Our love-hate relationship with our currency

insights.claim: Iceland's business and finance community is fixated on the growth gap between the EU and the US (citing Mario Draghi's competitiveness report) as evidence that full EU membership would risk Iceland's relative economic outperformance, a narrative that dominates over broader well-being comparisons even among those with direct experience of European quality of life.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a single competitiveness narrative (Draghi report) has become a self-reinforcing culture-war talking point well beyond its original economic-policy audience.

insights.claim: Despite the Ukraine war and Trump's threats against Greenland dominating international coverage of the referendum, none of it moved the campaign, which was fought almost entirely on domestic issues - a disconnect the author attributes to Icelanders being 'in denial' about how serious recent international developments are, per journalist Bogi Ágústsson.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Public risk perception in a NATO member state is lagging elite/expert assessment of the security environment, a gap that could delay defense-spending or policy responses until a shock forces recalibration.
insights.locator: The old order still looks solid from the North Atlantic

insights.claim: The Icelandic government moved the referendum forward from a planned 2027 specifically because of deteriorating international security developments, yet security and NATO concerns were not top of mind for voters during the actual campaign.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Highlights a mismatch between government threat assessment and public salience that could recur in other small NATO states facing similar referenda or elections.
insights.locator: The government had brought the referendum forward

insights.claim: The no campaign used culture-war tactics including micro-targeting young voters on social media and phone calls with claims that EU accession could lead to conscription into a 'European army,' while the yes side made its own unsupported claims about euro adoption easing housing access.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Shows referendum campaigns in small, stable democracies are now importing the same disinformation/micro-targeting playbook seen in larger populist campaigns.
insights.locator: That being said, there is no denying

insights.claim: The author warns that the referendum campaign's effective use of crisis framing, emotional micro-targeting and unsupported claims could become a reusable political blueprint for future Icelandic elections, eroding the country's historically civil political culture and public trust in elections.
insights.speaker: Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir
insights.so_what: Flags a durable second-order political-risk channel (campaign-tactic contagion) independent of the referendum's substantive outcome.
insights.quote: As any fisherman knows, illegal bait might get you an easier catch a few times, but eventually will ruin the fishing for all.
